pages.title: 🧭 00 — Learning Map & Decision Framework
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3cd3906c5d6c810c9e01e8ca9ac89172 as of 2026-09-23T21:32:01.261Z: {"title":"00 — Learning Map & Decision Framework"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"🧭"} ## خريطة بصرية السؤال الأول مش اسم الدالة. السؤال: الصف الواحد في النتيجة يمثل إيه؟ ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["What should one output row represent?"] --> C["More columns from a related table"] Q --> E["Do related rows exist?"] Q --> G["One row per group"] Q --> W["Keep every detail row and add a value"] Q --> S["Stack compatible rows"] Q --> N["Name the steps"] C --> JOIN["JOIN"] E --> EX["EXISTS"] G --> GB["GROUP BY"] W --> WIN["Window function"] S --> SET["UNION / INTERSECT / EXCEPT"] N --> CTE["CTE"] ``` شكل النتيجة واحد من دول: قيمة واحدة، صفوف كتيرة، صف لكل مجموعة، أو نفس الصفوف مع قيمة تحليلية. > صفحة البداية السريعة للمكتبة: كيف أختار تقنية SQL المناسبة، وكيف أراجع الاستعلام قبل أن أثق في نتيجته. # 1. SQL Problem-Solving Workflow ```txt Business Question ↓ Define Population ↓ Define Grain ↓ Identify required tables / relationships ↓ JOIN / Filter ↓ Transform: CASE / Subquery / CTE ↓ Aggregate or Window ↓ Validate result shape ↓ Validate edge cases + NULLs ↓ Check execution plan when needed ``` # 2. Choose the Technique | Need | Usually start with | | --- | --- | | Categorize rows | CASE | | Filter by a scalar/list produced by another query | Subquery in WHERE | | Build an intermediate table-like result | Derived Table / CTE | | Check whether related rows exist | EXISTS | | Row-by-row dependency on the outer query | Correlated Subquery | | Keep detail rows while adding an aggregate | Window Function | | Combine attributes from related tables | JOIN | | Multi-stage, readable transformation | CTE | # 3. The Grain Check Before writing SQL, finish this sentence: > One output row represents . Then verify that every JOIN and aggregation preserves or intentionally changes that grain. # 4. The Population Check Ask: - What rows enter the calculation? - Which rows are excluded before CASE/AVG/SUM? - What becomes NULL? - What exactly is the denominator? This is especially important for percentages and conditional aggregation. # 5. Result-Shape Checklist ```txt Scalar → one value Rowset → many rows Grouped result → one row per group Window result → original rows + analytic value Derived table / CTE → named intermediate rowset ``` # 6. Common Logic Traps - ELSE 0 can corrupt averages and percentages when non-target rows should be excluded. - COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(expression) ignores NULL expressions. - AVG() of raw rows is not the same as average of already aggregated groups. - A JOIN can multiply rows and silently inflate aggregates. - A correlated subquery may be logically correct but expensive; inspect the execution plan when scale matters. # 7. Final Review Questions 1. Is the business definition unambiguous? 2. Is the grain explicit? 3. Is the population correct? 4. Are NULL semantics intentional? 5. Is the denominator correct? 6. Could a JOIN multiply rows? 7. Would a CTE or window function make the intent clearer? 8. Have I tested edge cases? 9. Does the result reconcile to an independent calculation?

pages.title: 🧱 01 — SQL Foundations — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c81f698afea76e9396474 as of 2026-09-23T21:28:08.482Z: {"title":"01 — SQL Foundations — Complete Reference"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"🧱"} ## خريطة بصرية ده ترتيب المعنى، مش ترتيب تنفيذ المحرك. Window functions تتحسب بعد التجميع، فمش بتتفلتر جوه WHERE. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1 FROM / JOIN"] --> B["2 WHERE"] --> C["3 GROUP BY"] --> D["4 HAVING"] --> E["5 SELECT"] --> F["6 DISTINCT"] --> G["7 ORDER BY"] --> H["8 LIMIT"] ``` ## Purpose The canonical foundation for understanding SQL as a relational query language. This page owns the mental models that every later module depends on. ## 1. The SQL Mental Model SQL is declarative: you describe the result you want, while the database optimizer decides how to execute it. The most important distinction is between: - Logical query meaning — what rows/columns the query should return. - Physical execution — how the engine actually obtains that result. A strong SQL analyst reasons about both, especially when correctness and performance matter. ## 2. Tables, Rows, Columns, and Grain A table is a relation containing rows and attributes. Before writing a query, identify the grain: what one row represents. Examples: - orders: one row per order. - order_items: one row per order line. - student_term_snapshot: one row per student × term × active program. ### Why grain matters Many SQL bugs are not syntax bugs. They are grain mistakes that silently multiply rows or produce incorrect aggregates. Before JOIN, GROUP BY, or a window function, ask: > What does one input row represent, and what should one output row represent? ## 3. Logical Query Processing Order A useful conceptual order is: FROM / JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET Window functions are evaluated after the grouped result exists, which is why they can use aggregate results but generally cannot be used directly in WHERE. This order explains common patterns such as filtering a window-function result in an outer query or CTE. ## 4. SELECT Is Not "Just Choosing Columns" SELECT can: - project columns, - compute expressions, - evaluate scalar functions, - perform conditional logic, - calculate aggregates, - define window calculations. Example: ```sql SELECT product_id, quantity * unit_price AS revenue FROM order_items; ``` ## 5. WHERE vs HAVING WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. ```sql SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_spend FROM orders WHERE order_status = 'Completed' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000; ``` Interview trap: HAVING is not simply a "second WHERE". The two operate at different stages and grains. ## 6. NULL and Three-Valued Logic NULL means missing/unknown/not applicable; it is not the same as zero or an empty string. Comparisons involving NULL do not evaluate to ordinary TRUE/FALSE. SQL uses TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN. Correct checks: ```sql WHERE phone IS NULL WHERE phone IS NOT NULL ``` Incorrect: ```sql WHERE phone = NULL ``` Key functions/patterns: - COALESCE() for fallback values. - NULLIF() for converting a value to NULL conditionally. - COUNT(*) counts rows. - COUNT(column) ignores NULL values. ## 7. DISTINCT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the selected projection. Do not confuse: - removing duplicate output rows, - identifying duplicate business entities, - fixing row multiplication caused by an incorrect join. Using DISTINCT to hide a bad join is a correctness smell. ## 7.5 Keys (PK / FK / Candidate / Composite) - Primary key: uniquely identifies a row. - Foreign key: references a key in another table. - Candidate key: any minimal column set that could serve as a unique identifier. - Composite key: uniqueness requires multiple columns together. Understanding keys is a prerequisite for reasoning about JOIN cardinality (see Module 05). ## 7.6 Filtering Principles Prefer explicit, intention-revealing predicates: - range: amount >= 100 AND amount < 500 - membership: status IN ('Paid', 'Shipped') - pattern: name LIKE 'Am%' - null: discount IS NULL For timestamp ranges, prefer half-open intervals when appropriate: >= start AND < end. ## 8. Expressions, Aliases, and Reuse Column aliases improve readability, but alias visibility depends on SQL dialect and logical query stage. A select-list alias normally cannot be referenced by another expression in the same select list as though it were an already-materialized column. Prefer a CTE/derived table when a calculated result becomes an input to later logic. ## 9. Data Type Thinking SQL expressions are type-sensitive. Understand: - integer vs decimal/numeric, - text vs numeric, - date vs timestamp, - explicit casting, - implicit conversion rules, - integer division risks. Example: ```sql SELECT CAST(total_amount AS numeric) / NULLIF(order_count, 0) FROM ...; ``` ## 10. Determinism and Ordering A result set is not guaranteed to have a meaningful order unless ORDER BY is specified. Likewise, operations such as ROW_NUMBER() require an ordering definition if deterministic ranking is expected. Avoid assuming physical table order, insertion order, or clustered storage order is a logical ordering guarantee. ## 11. Core Safety Checks Before Aggregation Before writing a KPI query: 1. Define the population. 2. Define the grain. 3. Define the measure. 4. Define exclusions. 5. Check for NULLs. 6. Check join cardinality. 7. Validate row counts before and after joins. 8. Reconcile a sample against source records. ## 12. Common Anti-Patterns ### SELECT * Useful for exploration, risky in reusable production logic. ### DISTINCT as a band-aid May conceal duplicate-producing joins. ### Filtering after aggregation when row filtering was intended Can produce inefficient or semantically wrong queries. ### Comparing to NULL with = Produces no matches because NULL = NULL is not TRUE. ### Assuming row order Without ORDER BY, order is not guaranteed. ## 13. Mini Real-World Case Suppose management asks: > "What is the average completed-order value per customer in 2026?" A robust approach is: - establish the population: completed orders in 2026, - establish grain: one order per row before customer-level aggregation, - aggregate at customer grain, - calculate the desired metric at the correct level. The main lesson is that business definitions must precede SQL syntax. ## 14. Interview Traps Q: Why can WHERE not normally contain an aggregate like SUM(amount) > 1000? Because WHERE filters rows before grouping/aggregation. Use HAVING for group-level aggregate filters. Q: Why can a LEFT JOIN unexpectedly behave like an inner join? A predicate on the right-side table placed in WHERE can eliminate the NULL-extended rows created by the left join. Move the predicate into the ON condition when preserving unmatched left rows is required. Q: Why does COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(column)? COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values of that column. ## Ownership Rule This page owns foundational SQL reasoning. Other notes may reference these concepts, but should not duplicate the full canonical explanation.

pages.title: 🧩 02 — Database, Schema & Data Modeling — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c817bb98bd04baec48a17 as of 2026-09-04T00:15:15.217Z: {"title":"02 — Database, Schema & Data Modeling — Complete Reference"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"🧩"} > جزء من سلسلة Intermediate SQL: هذا المرجع مخصص لفهم بنية الـdatabase قبل أي تحليل — استكشاف الجداول، الـPK/FK والعلاقات، الـconstraints، وأساسيات التعامل مع NULL. # 1. سير عمل الاستكشاف الواقعي (The Real-World EDA Workflow) عندما تدخل Database جديدة في شغل حقيقي، لا تبدأ مباشرة بـ SELECT * على كل شيء. فكّر بالترتيب: ```txt Database ↓ 1. Discover tables & relationships ↓ 2. Inspect schema / ERD ↓ 3. Identify PKs & FKs ↓ 4. Understand data types & constraints ↓ 5. Sample rows ↓ 6. Check NULLs / missing / suspicious codes ↓ 7. Summarize distributions ↓ 8. Explore relationships between variables ↓ 9. Build intermediate datasets when useful ↓ 10. Answer the business question ``` ## مثال واقعي: Student Analytics Database تخيل أنك انضممت لفريق BI في جامعة، وعندك tables مثل students، enrollments، courses، departments. قبل أن تسأل "ما متوسط الـ GPA؟" لازم تعرف: ما هو الـgrain لكل table؟ ما هو الـprimary key؟ ما هي الـforeign keys؟ هل GPA يمكن أن يكون NULL؟ هل 0 GPA حقيقي أم missing code؟ > Core principle: فهم الـ semantics والـ schema يسبق التحليل. # 2. استكشاف محتوى الـDatabase ## 2.1 Database Client الـ database client هو البرنامج الذي تتصل من خلاله بالـ database وتنفذ SQL وتفحص الـ schema. يساعدك في اكتشاف Table names، Column names، Data types، Constraints، Relationships. > في الشغل الحقيقي، ارجع أيضًا إلى الـ ERD والـ data dictionary والـ database documentation؛ لا تعتمد على SQL وحده لفهم business meaning. ## 2.2 Sampling Rows ```sql SELECT customer_id, country, signup_date FROM customers LIMIT 10; ``` ### مهم الـ rows ليست مرتبة افتراضيًا. إذا كنت تريد ترتيبًا محددًا: ```sql SELECT * FROM customers ORDER BY signup_date DESC LIMIT 10; ``` > LIMIT يقلل عدد الصفوف المعروضة؛ لا يعني بالضرورة أن database قرأت فقط هذه الصفوف منطقياً في كل execution plan. # 3. أساسيات NULL NULL تعني unknown / missing value، وليست رقمًا ولا string فارغًا. ## 3.1 Correct NULL syntax ❌ خطأ: WHERE salary = NULL — ✅ صحيح: WHERE salary IS NULL وللبحث عن القيم الموجودة: WHERE salary IS NOT NULL ## 3.2 COUNT(\*) vs COUNT(column) COUNT(*) يعد عدد الصفوف. بينما COUNT(salary) يعد عدد القيم غير NULL فقط. إذن: ```txt Missing salary = COUNT(*) - COUNT(salary) ``` ### مثال واقعي: Data quality check ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows, COUNT(student_id) AS student_id_present, COUNT(gpa) AS gpa_present, COUNT(*) - COUNT(gpa) AS missing_gpa FROM students; ``` ## 3.3 COUNT(DISTINCT column) COUNT(DISTINCT country) يعد عدد القيم المختلفة غير NULL. لكن SELECT DISTINCT country FROM students; يمكن أن يظهر NULL كواحد من القيم المميزة. > Exam / interview trap: DISTINCT قد يعرض NULL، بينما COUNT(DISTINCT column) لا يعد NULL. # 4. المفاتيح والعلاقات (Keys & Relationships) ## 4.1 Primary Key (PK) الـ Primary Key هو العمود/مجموعة الأعمدة التي uniquely identify كل row. خصائصه: Unique، Not NULL، يحدد هوية الصف. ## 4.2 Foreign Key (FK) الـ Foreign Key هو column يشير إلى key في table أخرى، وغالبًا إلى primary key. ```txt students --------- id (PK) ↑ │ FK │ enrollments ------------ student_id (FK) ``` الـ FK يساعد على فرض referential integrity: القيمة الموجودة في الـ child table يجب أن تتوافق مع قيمة مسموحة في الـ referenced table، أو تكون NULL إذا كان العمود يسمح بذلك. ## 4.3 Self-reference ```txt employees --------- id PK manager_id FK → employees.id ``` يسمح بتمثيل hierarchy (CEO ← Manager ← Employees). ## 4.4 الـFK ليس شرطًا لعمل JOIN ```sql SELECT * FROM company c JOIN fortune500 f ON c.ticker = f.ticker; ``` إذا لم توجد FK بين الجدولين، فهذا لا يمنع الـ JOIN. الفرق أن database لا تفرض نفس referential constraint على ticker. > Key distinction: JOIN هو query operation؛ FOREIGN KEY هو database constraint. # 5. قيود الأعمدة (Column Constraints) الـ constraints تحدد ما القيم المسموح بها. ### UNIQUE كل قيمة غير NULL يجب أن تكون مختلفة: email TEXT UNIQUE ### NOT NULL العمود لا يقبل NULL: student_id INT NOT NULL ### CHECK يفرض business/data rule: CHECK (gpa >= 0 AND gpa <= 4) أو CHECK (end_date >= start_date) ### PK / FK PK يحدد row uniquely، FK يربط row بـ referenced row ويحافظ على referential integrity. > Important: Constraints are not the same as data types. Data type يحدد طبيعة القيم التي يمكن تخزينها؛ constraint يضيف قواعد إضافية على تلك القيم. # 6. أخطاء المقابلات والامتحانات - COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column): الأولى تعد الصفوف، الثانية تتجاهل NULL. - COUNT(DISTINCT column): يعد القيم المختلفة غير NULL فقط. - SELECT DISTINCT column: ممكن يرجع NULL كقيمة مميزة. - column = NULL: خطأ؛ استخدم IS NULL / IS NOT NULL. - FK vs JOIN: الـFK هو constraint؛ الـJOIN هو query operation. تقدر تعمل JOIN من غير FK. # 7. Cheat Sheet ```sql -- Sample SELECT * FROM table_name LIMIT 10; -- Missing SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(column_name) AS missing FROM table_name; -- Distinct values SELECT DISTINCT column_name FROM table_name; -- Distinct count SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT column_name) FROM table_name; ``` --- ### 🔗 مراجع ذات صلة

pages.title: 03 — Data Types, Casting & NULL Logic — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c81e78c92cb9d2ecf35ae as of 2026-09-10T19:05:43.804Z: {"title":"03 — Data Types, Casting & NULL Logic — Complete Reference"} null ## Purpose Canonical home for SQL data types, casting/conversion, NULL semantics, three-valued logic, and safe handling of missing/invalid values. ## 1. Data Type Mental Model A data type describes what values mean and what operations are valid. Choose types by business meaning, not by how the value happens to look. Common families: - Numeric: integer, decimal/numeric, floating point - Character: char, varchar, text - Temporal: date, time, timestamp, interval - Boolean - Dialect-specific types such as arrays, JSON, UUID ## 2. Exact vs Approximate Numbers Use numeric/decimal for values where exactness matters, especially financial amounts. Floating-point types are approximate and can introduce representation differences. ## 3. Casting Explicit casting makes transformations intentional: ```sql CAST(amount_text AS numeric) ``` PostgreSQL also supports: ```sql amount_text::numeric ``` Be careful: a cast can fail when source values are malformed. ## 4. NULL Is Not a Value NULL represents unknown, unavailable, or missing information. It is different from: - 0 - '' - FALSE Do not use = NULL or <> NULL.8 ```sql WHERE manager_id IS NULL ``` ## 5. Three-Valued Logic SQL predicates can evaluate to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. For example, 10 = NULL is UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause retains only TRUE rows. This explains many subtle filtering and anti-join bugs. ## 6. NULL Functions ### COALESCE Returns the first non-NULL expression. ```sql COALESCE(discount, 0) ``` ### NULLIF Returns NULL when two expressions are equal. ```sql NULLIF(quantity, 0) ``` Useful for preventing division by zero: ```sql revenue / NULLIF(quantity, 0) ``` ## 7. NULL in Aggregates COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX generally ignore NULL inputs, with result behavior depending on whether usable values exist. Always distinguish no rows, all NULL, and zero as business states. ## 8. NULL in JOINs NULL = NULL is not TRUE. Therefore rows with NULL join keys do not match using ordinary equality. When NULL-safe matching is required, use a dialect-appropriate approach intentionally. ## 9. NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS NOT IN can produce surprising results when its subquery contains NULL. For relational existence logic, NOT EXISTS is often safer and clearer. ## 10. Data Quality Pattern For raw data, separate: 1. invalid values; 2. missing values; 3. legitimate zero/empty values; 4. unknown/unavailable values. Do not blindly replace every NULL with zero. ## 11. Real-World BI Example A student dataset may contain NULL graduation dates for active students. Replacing them with an arbitrary date would corrupt cohort and completion analysis. Preserve NULL when it represents “not yet applicable.” ## 12. Common Traps - = NULL instead of IS NULL - COUNT(column) interpreted as row count - replacing NULL with zero without business meaning - NOT IN with nullable subqueries - integer division assumptions - silent/unsafe implicit casts - using floating point for exact financial calculations ## 13. Ownership This page is the canonical deep reference for Data Types, Casting, NULL, and three-valued logic. Other SQL notes should link here instead of reproducing the full theory. pages.title: 04 — Filtering & Conditional Logic — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c8141a33ce769f1a47973 as of 2026-09-01T20:05:39.863Z: {"title":"04 — Filtering & Conditional Logic — Complete Reference"} null ## Purpose Canonical home for row filtering, predicates, CASE expressions, conditional expressions, and the reasoning behind WHERE/HAVING/filter placement. ## 1. WHERE as Population Control WHERE defines which source rows enter the next logical stage of the query. ```sql SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed'; ``` Think of filtering as defining the analytical population. ## 2. Core Predicate Families - comparison: =, <>, >, >=, <, <= - range: BETWEEN - membership: IN - pattern: LIKE - NULL: IS NULL, IS NOT NULL - existence: EXISTS ## 3. AND / OR / NOT Use parentheses whenever business logic could be ambiguous. ```sql WHERE country = 'EG' AND (status = 'Active' OR status = 'Pending') ``` Do not rely on readers remembering operator precedence. ## 4. CASE CASE maps conditions to values. ```sql CASE WHEN amount >= 10000 THEN 'High Value' WHEN amount >= 5000 THEN 'Medium Value' ELSE 'Low Value' END ``` Use it for classification, conditional calculations, flags, and controlled business rules. ## 5. Simple vs Searched CASE Simple CASE compares one expression against values. ```sql CASE status WHEN 'A' THEN 'Active' WHEN 'I' THEN 'Inactive' END ``` Searched CASE evaluates independent conditions and is more flexible. ## 6. CASE in Aggregation A major analytical pattern: ```sql SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) ``` This is the bridge between conditional logic and KPI generation. ## 7. CASE and NULL Be explicit about NULL behavior. An unmatched CASE expression reaches ELSE, or returns NULL if no ELSE is supplied. ## 8. WHERE vs HAVING Use WHERE to reduce rows before grouping. Use HAVING to filter groups based on aggregate results. ## 9. Filter Placement with JOINs With LEFT JOIN, putting a right-table condition in WHERE can remove NULL-extended rows. Put the condition in ON when the intent is to preserve unmatched left rows. ## 10. Real-World Example Customer segmentation: - High value: lifetime revenue >= 50,000 - At risk: no completed order in 90 days - New: first order within 30 days Each classification should have an explicit population and precedence rule. ## 11. Interview Traps - WHERE vs HAVING - CASE without ELSE - overlapping CASE conditions - incorrect AND/OR precedence - filtering the right side of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE - confusing CASE with COALESCE ## 12. Ownership This page owns filtering and conditional logic. Deep subquery/CTE mechanics belong to Module 07; aggregation mechanics belong to Module 06.

pages.title: 🔗 05 — JOINs & Relationship Reasoning — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c81419b2fecc50db92f04 as of 2026-09-23T21:28:24.782Z: {"title":"05 — JOINs & Relationship Reasoning — Complete Reference"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"🔗"} ## خريطة بصرية لو العميل عنده أوردران مبالغهم 100 و 50، ودفعتان مبلغهم 80 و 70، الـ JOIN الخام يعمل 4 صفوف. مجموع مبلغ الأوردر على الصفوف دي يبقى 300 مش 150. ```mermaid flowchart TD R["What is the relationship?"] --> M["Many side joined to another many side"] R --> OK["Many side joined to one parent row"] M --> Fan["2 orders x 2 payments = 4 rows"] Fan --> Wrong["SUM of the order amount becomes 300"] M --> Fix["Aggregate each child table to the parent grain first"] Fix --> Right["Then join the summaries: orders 150, payments 150"] OK --> Check["Still compare row count before and after the join"] ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD L["LEFT JOIN"] --> On["Right-table filter in ON"] L --> Wh["Right-table filter in WHERE"] On --> Keep["Unmatched left rows stay"] Wh --> Lose["Unmatched left rows disappear"] ``` ## Purpose The canonical reference for JOINs, relationship semantics, cardinality, row multiplication, and join correctness. ## 1. The Core Mental Model A JOIN combines rows from two row sets according to a matching condition. The most important question is not "which JOIN syntax should I use?" but: > What relationship exists between the two row sets, and what output grain do I need? ## 2. Cardinality Typical relationship patterns: - 1:1 — one row on each side matches one row. - 1:M — one parent row matches many child rows. - M:1 — many child rows map to one parent. - M:M — many rows can match many rows. A JOIN can increase row count. That is not automatically wrong; it is a consequence of the relationship. ## 3. INNER JOIN Returns only matched rows. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id; ``` Use when unmatched rows are irrelevant or intentionally excluded. ## 4. LEFT JOIN Returns every row from the left side, with matching right-side data where available. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id; ``` Use for questions such as: > Which customers have no orders? ```sql WHERE o.order_id IS NULL ``` ## 5. RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOIN RIGHT JOIN preserves the right side; it is often rewritten as a LEFT JOIN by swapping table positions for readability. FULL OUTER JOIN preserves unmatched rows from both sides and is useful for reconciliation/matching problems. ## 6. CROSS JOIN Produces the Cartesian product of two row sets. If A has 100 rows and B has 20 rows, a pure Cartesian product has 2,000 rows. Use intentionally for scenarios such as generating combinations, calendars, scenarios, or cohort × metric matrices. Accidental cross joins are a serious correctness/performance problem. ## 7. Join Conditions A robust join condition should express the true business relationship. Example composite relationship: ```sql ON a.student_id = b.student_id AND a.term_code = b.term_code ``` Joining on only one component can create false matches. ## 8. One-to-Many Aggregation Trap Suppose customers has one row per customer and orders has many rows per customer. This is valid: ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id; ``` But joining orders to another one-to-many table such as payments may multiply rows. Example: - customer has 3 orders, - customer has 2 payments, - joining both raw child tables by customer can create up to 6 combinations. This is the classic fan-out / row multiplication problem. ## 9. The Safe Aggregation Pattern Aggregate each many-side independently before joining when the business grain requires it. ```sql WITH order_totals AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(order_amount) AS total_orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ), payment_totals AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(payment_amount) AS total_payments FROM payments GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT c.customer_id, COALESCE(o.total_orders, 0) AS total_orders, COALESCE(p.total_payments, 0) AS total_payments FROM customers c LEFT JOIN order_totals o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id LEFT JOIN payment_totals p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id; ``` ## 10. JOIN vs EXISTS Use a JOIN when you need columns from the related table or need to combine row sets. Use EXISTS when the question is primarily: > Does at least one related row exist? ```sql SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id ); ``` This avoids creating duplicate customer rows merely to test existence. ## 11. LEFT JOIN + WHERE Trap This: ```sql FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'Completed' ``` can remove customers with no matching orders. When preserving all customers is required, consider: ```sql FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'Completed' ``` ## 11.5 JOIN vs IN IN expresses membership in a set. EXISTS expresses existence of a related row and is often safer for correlated relational logic. Be careful with NULL semantics when comparing NOT IN against NOT EXISTS — NOT IN against a set containing NULL can silently return zero rows. ## 12. Joining on Nullable Columns Ordinary equality does not match NULL to NULL. If business semantics require treating two missing values as a match, use an explicit dialect-appropriate null-safe comparison strategy and document it. ## 13. Self JOIN A table can be joined to itself. Example employee-manager hierarchy: ```sql SELECT e.employee_name, m.employee_name AS manager_name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id; ``` ## 14. Bridge Tables and Many-to-Many Relationships A many-to-many relationship is often represented through a bridge/junction table. Example: students ↔ student_courses ↔ courses Never assume a direct many-to-many join preserves a unique row grain. ## 15. Join Validation Checklist After a new JOIN, compare: - row count before vs after, - distinct business keys before vs after, - unmatched rows, - duplicate keys on either side, - expected cardinality, - aggregates before vs after. A strong analyst treats join validation as part of query development, not a final cleanup step. ## 16. Real BI / DWH Case In a warehouse, joining a fact table to dimensions is normally many-to-one from fact to dimension. If a supposedly unique dimension key matches multiple dimension rows, the fact can multiply and KPIs can be overstated. Therefore, referential integrity and dimension uniqueness are analytical correctness controls, not just database administration concerns. ## 17. Interview Traps Q: Why did my total revenue double after adding a JOIN? Likely row multiplication caused by a one-to-many or many-to-many relationship. Inspect the grain and cardinality instead of adding DISTINCT blindly. Q: JOIN or EXISTS for "customers who placed at least one order"? EXISTS is often the clearer expression because the requirement is existence, not returning order columns. Q: Can LEFT JOIN increase rows? Yes. LEFT describes preservation of left rows; it does not guarantee one output row per left row. ## Ownership Rule This page owns JOIN semantics, cardinality, row multiplication, and join correctness. Other modules may use examples but should link back here for deep reasoning. CASE Statements — Complete Reference

pages.title: 📊 06 — Aggregation & Grouping — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c813a95abc3b25b698b3e as of 2026-09-23T21:32:23.107Z: {"title":"06 — Aggregation & Grouping — Complete Reference"} {"type":"emoji","emoji":"📊"} ## خريطة بصرية WHERE يشيل صفوف. GROUP BY يغيّر الـ grain لصف واحد لكل مجموعة. HAVING يشيل مجموعات. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Input rows"] --> B["WHERE"] --> C["GROUP BY"] --> D["HAVING"] --> E["One row per group"] ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Do you still need the detail rows?"] --> No["No"] Q --> Yes["Yes"] No --> GB["GROUP BY"] Yes --> Win["Window function"] GB --> Note["An average of averages is wrong when the groups have different sizes"] ``` ## Purpose The canonical reference for GROUP BY, aggregate functions, grain transitions, conditional aggregation, and KPI-safe aggregation. ## 1. Aggregation Is a Grain Transformation The deepest way to understand aggregation is: > GROUP BY transforms many input rows into one output row per group key. Example: - Input grain: one row per order. - GROUP BY customer_id. - Output grain: one row per customer. Every selected expression must therefore be compatible with the new group grain. ## 2. Core Aggregate Functions Common aggregates: - COUNT - SUM - AVG - MIN - MAX - dialect-specific statistical/percentile functions Example: ```sql SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(amount) AS revenue, AVG(amount) AS avg_order_value FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; ``` ## 3. COUNT(\*) vs COUNT(column) COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. This distinction matters whenever a column can be missing. ## 4. SUM and NULL SUM(column) ignores NULL inputs, but a group containing only NULL values may produce a NULL result rather than zero depending on dialect behavior. Use explicit business semantics: ```sql COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) ``` when zero is the correct interpretation. ## 5. AVG Is Not Always the Average You Think An average of averages can be wrong when subgroup sizes differ. Incorrect idea: ```txt (average of group A + average of group B) / 2 ``` Correct overall average requires weighting by the number of observations or aggregating the underlying numerator/denominator correctly. ## 6. GROUP BY and Selected Columns A selected non-aggregated column generally must be part of the grouping set or otherwise be functionally determined in a dialect-supported way. Conceptually: > Every output row must have an unambiguous value for every selected expression. ## 7. WHERE vs HAVING Use WHERE to remove input rows before grouping. Use HAVING to filter resulting groups. ```sql SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 10000; ``` ## 8. Conditional Aggregation One of the most useful SQL patterns for BI/analytics. ```sql SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_orders, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS completed_orders, SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_orders FROM orders; ``` For amounts: ```sql SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) ``` This pattern turns row-level conditions into multiple KPIs in one grouped query. ## 8.5 COUNT vs SUM(CASE) For counts of conditions, these two forms can express the same business idea: ```sql COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 END) ``` ```sql SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) ``` But NULL behavior and readability should be considered when choosing between them. ## 9. DISTINCT Aggregation COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) answers a different question from COUNT(*). Example: > Number of unique customers who placed an order. ```sql SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM orders; ``` Do not confuse row count with entity count. ## 10. GROUP BY Multiple Dimensions ```sql SELECT college_code, term_code, COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) AS students FROM enrollment GROUP BY college_code, term_code; ``` Output grain becomes: one row per college × term. This explicit grain statement is extremely useful for validating BI datasets. ## 11. Aggregation After JOIN Always reason about whether the JOIN has changed the grain before aggregation. Dangerous: ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, SUM(o.amount) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id; ``` If multiple payments exist per customer, order rows may multiply. Safer pattern: aggregate each many-side to the required grain before joining. ## 12. Semi-Additive Measures Not every metric can be summed across every dimension. Examples: - transaction revenue is usually additive across transactions/time, - account balance may be additive across accounts but not across time, - inventory balance often should use an end-of-period or snapshot logic rather than summing daily balances. Correct KPI design requires knowing the measure's additivity properties. ## 13. Grouping Sets, ROLLUP, and CUBE Advanced grouping features can generate multiple aggregation levels in one query. Concepts: - ROLLUP — hierarchical subtotals. - CUBE — combinations of grouping dimensions. - GROUPING SETS — explicitly requested grouping levels. Example: ```sql SELECT region, product_category, SUM(revenue) FROM sales GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product_category); ``` These are especially useful for reporting and multidimensional summaries. ## 14. Aggregation vs Window Functions GROUP BY reduces rows. Window functions calculate across related rows while preserving the detail rows. Example: ```sql -- Aggregation: one row per customer SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; ``` versus: ```sql -- Window: keeps one row per order SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total FROM orders; ``` This distinction is one of the most important interview concepts in analytical SQL. ## 15. KPI Design Pattern Before writing a KPI, define: Numerator → what counts toward the metric? Denominator → what is the comparison population? Grain → what is one observation? Population filters → which rows are eligible? Null treatment → missing, zero, excluded, or unknown? Join effects → can relationships multiply rows? Example conversion rate: ```txt successful_orders / eligible_orders ``` Do not calculate a ratio until both numerator and denominator populations are explicitly defined. ## 16. Real BI Case — Enrollment Suppose management asks for: > Active students by college and academic term. Input grain may be one student × term × program. If the business KPI is one student counted once per college × term, using COUNT(*) could overcount students enrolled in multiple programs. The correct metric may require: ```sql COUNT(DISTINCT student_id) ``` The business grain determines the SQL. ## 17. Validation Techniques For a new aggregate: - compare total rows to source expectations, - compare COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT business_key), - reconcile totals to a trusted report, - inspect a small sample manually, - test edge cases involving NULLs and duplicate keys. ## 18. Interview Traps Q: Why is COUNT(*) sometimes wrong for "customers"? Because rows may represent transactions, not customers. Use the count that matches the business entity, often COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id). Q: Why did SUM(revenue) increase after a JOIN? Usually because the JOIN multiplied fact rows before aggregation. Q: GROUP BY or window function? Use GROUP BY when you need fewer rows at a new grain. Use a window function when you need an analytical calculation while preserving row detail. ## 17.5 Common Analytical Mistakes (Checklist) - counting rows instead of entities; - averaging already-aggregated averages; - summing duplicated facts after a JOIN; - filtering with HAVING when WHERE could reduce data earlier; - forgetting NULL behavior; - mixing columns from incompatible grains; - grouping by too many columns and unintentionally producing a lower-level grain. ## Ownership Rule This page owns aggregation semantics, grouping, KPI-safe aggregation, grain transitions, and conditional aggregation.

pages.title: 07 — Subqueries & CTEs — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c81d68b7ef8df11ee0d7d as of 2026-09-23T21:28:35.908Z: {"title":"07 — Subqueries & CTEs — Complete Reference"} null ## خريطة بصرية شكل الاستعلام الداخلي هو اللي يحدد الأداة، مش مكانه في الجملة. ```mermaid flowchart TD S["What does the inner query return?"] --> Scalar["One value"] S --> List["Many values, one column"] S --> Rel["Rows and columns"] S --> Row["It depends on the current outer row"] Scalar --> A["Scalar subquery"] List --> B["IN"] Rel --> C["Derived table or CTE"] Row --> D["Correlated subquery"] D --> E["Use EXISTS when the question is only existence"] ``` CTE بتسمي الخطوة. مش جدول مؤقت، ومش أسرع تلقائي. ## Purpose Canonical home for SQL subqueries and Common Table Expressions (CTEs), with emphasis on grain, scope, correlation, execution behavior, readability, and choosing the right pattern. ## 1. Core Mental Model A subquery is a query nested inside another query. The important question is not merely where it appears, but what shape it returns and how the outer query consumes it. Think in four shapes: - Scalar → one value - Single-column list → many values from one column - Derived table → rows and columns used as a relation - Correlated subquery → evaluated logically in relation to the current outer row ## 2. Subquery in WHERE Use when the business question is about membership or existence. ```sql SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE customer_id IN ( SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01' ); ``` ### IN vs EXISTS - IN expresses membership in a returned set. - EXISTS expresses whether at least one matching row exists. - For anti-matching, prefer NOT EXISTS when NULL behavior could make NOT IN unsafe. ## 3. Scalar Subquery in SELECT A scalar subquery returns one value per outer row. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id, c.customer_name, (SELECT MAX(o.order_date) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order_date FROM customers c; ``` Use it when the relationship is naturally one value per outer row. If the logic becomes complex or expensive, consider a JOIN or pre-aggregation. ## 4. Derived Tables A subquery in FROM becomes a temporary relational result for the outer query. ```sql SELECT customer_id, total_sales FROM ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ) s WHERE total_sales > 100000; ``` This is especially useful when you must aggregate first, then filter or join. ## 5. Correlated Subqueries A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query. ```sql SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.amount > 10000 ); ``` The key idea is row-relative logic: the inner condition depends on the current outer row. ## 6. Nested Subqueries A nested subquery contains another subquery. Nesting is valid, but deep nesting can hide business intent. Prefer a CTE or staged transformation when each logical step deserves a name. ## 7. CTEs A CTE names an intermediate query using WITH. ```sql WITH customer_sales AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total_sales FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT * FROM customer_sales WHERE total_sales > 100000; ``` CTEs improve readability, decomposition, reuse within a statement, and debugging. They are primarily a query-organization mechanism; do not assume a CTE automatically materializes or improves performance in every database. ## 8. Multiple CTEs Use sequential CTEs when the analytical problem has clear stages. ```sql WITH monthly_sales AS ( SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month, customer_id, SUM(amount) AS sales FROM orders GROUP BY 1, 2 ), ranked AS ( SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY sales DESC) AS rnk FROM monthly_sales ) SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 10; ``` ## 9. Subquery vs CTE vs JOIN vs Window Function | Technique | Best fit | | --- | --- | | JOIN | Bring related attributes/rows together | | EXISTS | Test whether a related row exists | | IN | Membership in a set | | Scalar subquery | One value per outer row | | Derived table | Transform rows before outer query | | CTE | Name and stage complex logic | | Window function | Compare a row with related rows without collapsing grain | ## 10. Grain Is the Deciding Factor Before writing the query, state the grain. Example: - Source grain: one row per order line. - Required result: one row per customer. If you aggregate inside a subquery/CTE before joining to customers, you can control row multiplication and preserve the intended grain. ## 11. Real BI Use Case — Student Analytics Business question: Which students are currently active and have completed more credits than the average active student? ```sql WITH active_students AS ( SELECT student_id, earned_hours FROM enrollment_snapshot WHERE status_code = 'ACTIVE' ), avg_hours AS ( SELECT AVG(earned_hours) AS avg_earned_hours FROM active_students ) SELECT s.student_id, s.earned_hours FROM active_students s CROSS JOIN avg_hours a WHERE s.earned_hours > a.avg_earned_hours; ``` The CTE separates population definition from benchmark calculation, making the logic easier to validate. ## 12. Correctness Checks Before trusting a subquery/CTE solution: 1. What is the outer-query grain? 2. What shape does the inner query return? 3. Can the inner query return multiple rows where a scalar is expected? 4. Can NULL change the result of IN / NOT IN? 5. Will a JOIN be clearer or safer? 6. Does the transformation accidentally multiply rows? 7. Can each stage be validated independently? ## 13. Performance Notes - Reduce rows early when appropriate. - Pre-aggregate before joining when the target grain is higher than the source grain. - Use execution plans rather than assuming a CTE/subquery is faster. - Correlated logic can be elegant but should be measured on large datasets. - Index/filter columns that participate in selective predicates and joins where appropriate. ## 14. Interview Traps - A CTE is not automatically a temporary table. - A CTE is not automatically faster than an equivalent subquery. - EXISTS checks existence; it does not need to return the matching values. - A scalar subquery must logically produce at most one value for each outer row. - NOT IN can behave unexpectedly when the subquery contains NULL. - DISTINCT should not be used as a blind fix for row multiplication. ## 15. Canonical Ownership This page is the single canonical reference for Subqueries and CTEs. Legacy pages should preserve useful examples and applied material, but should point back here for the complete conceptual treatment. Simple Subqueries — Complete Reference Correlated Subqueries — Complete Reference Nested Subqueries — Complete Reference Common Table Expressions (CTEs) — Complete Reference Choosing the Right SQL Technique + Final Case Study

pages.title: 08 — Set Operations — Complete Reference
pages.text: Here is the result of "fetch" for the Page with URL https://app.notion.com/p/3ce3906c5d6c81b7baa9e32203cdbeb0 as of 2026-09-23T21:29:12.673Z: {"title":"08 — Set Operations — Complete Reference"} null ## خريطة بصرية Current = 1, 2, 3. Archived = 3, 4. UNION ALL يسيب الـ 3 مرتين. INTERSECT يرجّع 3 فقط. EXCEPT يرجّع 1 و 2. ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["What are you combining?"] --> Col["Columns from a related table"] Q --> Rows["Compatible rows from two results"] Col --> Join["JOIN"] Rows --> All["UNION ALL: keep duplicates"] Rows --> U["UNION: drop duplicate rows"] Rows --> I["INTERSECT: rows in both"] Rows --> X["EXCEPT: rows in the first result only"] ``` ## Purpose Canonical reference for combining result sets with UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT. ## 1. Set Operations vs JOINs JOIN combines columns across related rows. Set operations combine rows from compatible result sets. This distinction is fundamental. ## 2. UNION vs UNION ALL UNION combines result sets and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL combines them without deduplication and is usually preferable when duplicates are meaningful or impossible by design. ```sql SELECT customer_id FROM current_customers UNION ALL SELECT customer_id FROM archived_customers; ``` ## 3. Column Compatibility Corresponding SELECT statements must have compatible numbers and types of columns. Column names are taken from the first query in the set operation. ## 4. INTERSECT Returns rows present in both result sets. Useful for finding overlap between populations. ## 5. EXCEPT Returns rows present in the first result set but absent from the second. Useful for gap analysis and reconciliation. ## 6. Real-World BI Use Cases - current vs archived customer populations - students enrolled in both programs - reconciliation between source and warehouse IDs - identifying records present in source A but missing from source B ## 7. UNION vs JOIN Decision Ask: - Need more columns from related records? → JOIN. - Need to stack compatible rows? → UNION/UNION ALL. - Need overlap? → INTERSECT. - Need difference? → EXCEPT / anti-join pattern. ## 8. Common Traps - using UNION when UNION ALL is intended - mismatched column meaning despite compatible data types - assuming UNION preserves duplicates - confusing set difference with a LEFT JOIN anti-join ## 9. Ownership This page is the canonical deep reference for SQL set operations.
